candidate.blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — STI prevention education
candidate.educational_objective: Teach evidence-based STI risk-reduction strategies and correct misconceptions about asymptomatic infection and the limits of condom protection.

options.A: Use condoms correctly every time, discuss STI testing and results with partners and the health care provider, and receive indicated vaccines such as HPV or hepatitis B when eligible.
options.B: If a partner looks healthy and has no symptoms, STI testing and safer-sex practices are unnecessary.
options.C: Condoms eliminate the risk of every STI, including infections transmitted through uncovered skin-to-skin contact.
options.D: STI prevention is relevant only after symptoms appear because asymptomatic infections cannot be transmitted.

candidate.rationale: CDC prevention guidance recommends safer-sex strategies such as correct condom use, appropriate STI testing, communication with partners and health care providers, and vaccination for preventable infections such as HPV and hepatitis B when indicated. Many STIs can be asymptomatic, so lack of symptoms does not establish that a person is uninfected. Condoms reduce risk but do not provide absolute protection against all infections, especially those spread by skin-to-skin contact.
candidate.source_claim_supported: CDC recommends a combination of safer-sex practices, risk-appropriate testing, partner/provider communication, and indicated vaccination; asymptomatic infection is possible and condoms reduce but do not eliminate all STI risk.
